examples.before:
Toroidal diamagnetic magnetic flux at an inside flux surface is the diamagnetic contribution to the [toroidal magnetic flux] through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a selected closed flux surface. It is a surface-dependent cumulative flux inside the plasma boundary, not only a boundary value.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, let $S_\chi$ be the constant-$\phi$ poloidal cross-section enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\chi$. With $d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \hat{\phi}\,dA$ oriented toward increasing $\phi$, the enclosed diamagnetic toroidal flux is defined by:

$$
\Phi_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(\chi) = \int_{S_\chi} \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z) \cdot d\mathbf{A}_\phi = \int_{S_\chi} B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}(R,Z)\,dA
$$

where $\chi$ identifies the selected flux surface, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the equilibrium magnetic field, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is its toroidal component, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle, and $dA$ is the positive scalar area element on $S_\chi$.

This quantity includes only the diamagnetic magnetic-field contribution. It is distinct from the total [toroidal_magnetic_flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which includes all magnetic-field contributions, from [toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is evaluated at the plasma boundary, and from [toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current), which isolates the poloidal-current contribution at that boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the net diamagnetic magnetic-field contribution through the enclosed poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

examples.before:
Local total magnetic-induction vector is the magnetic flux-density vector at a point, carrying both the local field direction and field strength. It is the unqualified parent quantity before selecting a source contribution, perturbation state, component, scalar reduction, spatial aggregation, or evaluation locus.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the vector resolves into radial, toroidal, and vertical components as

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_\phi\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_Z\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is this local total magnetic-induction vector; $B_R$ is its radial projection, $B_\phi$ is its [toroidal magnetic-field component](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and $B_Z$ is its [vertical magnetic-field component](name:vertical_magnetic_field); and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ are the corresponding basis vectors. The frame is right-handed with $\hat{\mathbf{R}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{Z}}$; $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies wherever a local magnetic induction is defined, including confined plasma and surrounding vacuum regions, and no particle species or population is selected or aggregated. It is pointwise and vector-valued: it is not the [magnetic field magnitude], a [flux-surface-average magnetic field], or an extremum such as the [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field). No cylindrical component, source contribution, perturbation state, or named locus is implied by the unqualified name.

When a [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$ is used, $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator, and a gage change affects $\mathbf{A}$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$. Source-qualified fields such as the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) and [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field) are vector contributions of the same kind and add vectorially when they belong to the same electromagnetic state; the [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the toroidal projection of the vacuum contribution. The [reference magnetic field](name:reference_magnetic_field) is a reference total magnetic-induction vector of the same kind, not a source-specific contribution; the [toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) is the toroidal projection evaluated at the magnetic-axis locus.

Sign convention: Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

A momentum source density represents the directed transfer of momentum caused by physical processes acting on a plasma population or one of its resolved states. It may retain vector direction or represent a selected component of the momentum-transfer rate.

The area-normalized source is defined by

$$
\mathbf{S}_{p} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{src}}}{\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{src}}$ is the momentum transferred by the source processes, $A$ is the surface over which the source is normalized, and $t$ is time. Concrete variants may resolve a radial component, an internal state, or an ion charge state, as in [radial momentum source] and [ion charge-state momentum source](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_source). Population-level quantities may sum the corresponding state-resolved contributions, as for [ion momentum source](name:ion_momentum_source).

examples.before:
The magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ is a gage-dependent vector field characterizing the electromagnetic state of a plasma. It enters fundamental physics through the canonical particle momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A}$, where $m$ is particle mass and $q$ is particle charge, and it governs inductive electromagnetic effects in both equilibrium and perturbed plasma states.

The defining relation connecting $\mathbf{A}$ to the magnetic induction $\mathbf{B}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic induction. Only the curl of $\mathbf{A}$ is directly physical; the vector potential itself is gage dependent. Its time derivative contributes to the inductive electric field via $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{ind} = -\partial\mathbf{A}/\partial t$, which is central to Faraday's law in electromagnetic plasma models.

Specific projections serve distinct physical roles. The field-aligned component $A_\parallel = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}$ is the equilibrium field unit vector, governs Alfvénic dynamics and is the component retained in gyrokinetic and reduced-MHD formulations; [its normalized perturbed amplitude] is used in eigenmode studies. Cylindrical components in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — radial, toroidal, and vertical — are natural for equilibrium and MHD calculations, while the poloidal projection in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$ arises in neoclassical transport analyzes. In vacuum regions, $\mathbf{A}$ is generated solely by external coil currents, with no plasma-current contribution.

Momentum convection velocity is an effective velocity coefficient for advective, non-diffusive transport of momentum carried by a specified neutral species. Its neutral-species form aggregates momentum over all resolved neutral internal states and is distinct from the material bulk velocity.

For a resolved transport direction $i$ and transported momentum component $j$, the advective contribution to the momentum-flux tensor is defined by:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{adv}}_{ij}=V_iP_j
$$

where $P_j$ is the selected momentum-density component, $\Pi^{\mathrm{adv}}_{ij}$ is its advective flux, and $V_i$ is the corresponding effective transport velocity. For a vector quantity, the resolved $V_i$ values form the effective transport-velocity vector.

The coefficient applies only to the selected neutral species, momentum component, and transport direction; it excludes diffusive transport, external source terms, and the material bulk velocity. It is the neutral-species realization of [momentum convection velocity]. The [toroidal neutral-species form](name:toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) and [vertical neutral-species form](name:vertical_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) show that the component label identifies the transported momentum in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, not necessarily the direction of the effective velocity.

examples.before:
Plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the plasma, the scalar part of the kinetic pressure tensor in a fluid or magnetohydrodynamic description. It represents equilibrium mechanical stress from the plasma populations included in the pressure model and is not a perturbation amplitude.

The scalar pressure is the one-third trace of the kinetic pressure tensor:

$$
p = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}
$$

where $p$ is the plasma pressure, $\mathbf{P}$ is the kinetic pressure tensor, and $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the tensor trace. For locally isotropic Maxwellian populations, an included population $s$ contributes $n_s k_B T_s$, where $n_s$ is the number density of population $s$, $T_s$ is its temperature, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

The unqualified quantity applies to equilibrium scalar kinetic pressure; it is additive over the included plasma populations and does not imply normalization, volume integration, or selection of only a bulk-thermal, fast-particle, or perturbed population subset. It excludes magnetic pressure, dynamic ram pressure, anisotropic pressure components, and any individual component of the pressure tensor.

[Total plasma pressure](name:total_plasma_pressure) is the specialization in which all represented equilibrium kinetic pressure contributions are included, while [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) is restricted to bulk thermal electron and ion populations. [Perturbed plasma pressure] denotes a first-order variation about an equilibrium pressure and is not part of the equilibrium quantity defined here. In magnetohydrostatic equilibrium, the pressure gradient satisfies $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\nabla p$ is the spatial gradient of plasma pressure, $\mathbf{j}$ is the electric current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field; on nested magnetic flux surfaces this pressure may be expressed as a function of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$, where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

This quantity is the net local volumetric energy exchange caused by Coulomb collisions for a designated target population. It is positive for energy deposited in the target and negative for energy transferred from it.

$$
P_a^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_b Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_a^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the target power density in W m$^{-3}$, $Q_{a\leftarrow b}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional energy-transfer rate per unit volume from partner population $b$ to target $a$, and the sum includes the collision partners and subpopulations specified by the quantity's aggregation scope.

The target may be a broad population, as in [particle collisional power density], or a species, ion charge state, internal state, or electron population. Aggregated electron and ion quantities include the designated contributing species and states, whereas resolved quantities retain only their specified target, as in [ion charge-state collisional power density](name:ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [internal-state collisional power density].

Sign convention: Positive when the designated target population gains energy from its collision partners.

This quantity is the volume-integrated net rate of energy transfer into the complete ion population from Coulomb scattering interactions with all colliding plasma constituents. As a structural abstraction within the collisional-power family, it aggregates thermal and fast ion receiving populations across all ion species and charge states without resolving which ion sub-population receives the energy.

The volume-integrated ion collisional power is defined as:

$$
P_{\rm ion,coll} = \int_V Q_{\rm ion,coll}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_{\rm ion,coll}$ is the local [ion power density due to collisions](name:ion_power_density_due_to_collisions) into the aggregate ion receiving population and the integral extends over the plasma volume $V$.

The receiving population is charge-state-summed for each ion species and species-summed over the ion population. Collisional exchanges among ion sub-populations contained in this aggregate cancel in the all-ion sum; the retained value is the net transfer between the aggregate ion population and populations outside that aggregate, including the complementary [electron power due to collisions]. Population-resolved components include [fast ion power due to collisions](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions), [thermal ion power due to collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions), and the charge-state-resolved [ion-state power due to collisions](name:total_ion_charge_state_power_due_to_collisions); [power due to collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) is the corresponding population-abstract parent.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb scattering interactions transfer net energy into the complete ion population.

examples.before:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as [poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop), which evaluates a flux function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, [reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux of flux loop], shares the same magnetic quantity but represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux loop.
examples.after:
Signed poloidal magnetic flux of a flux loop is the magnetic flux linked by an individual flux loop and threading an oriented surface whose boundary is that loop. It is the finite-surface flux linkage associated with the loop as a whole, not a local magnetic-field component.

The loop-linked flux is defined by the surface integral of the magnetic-field vector over a spanning surface of the loop:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{loop}}} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux of the flux loop, $S_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is an oriented spanning surface bounded by the flux loop, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the directed surface element on that surface.

The scope is one specified flux loop and the total flux through its complete spanning surface; no averaging over multiple loops or loop segments is implied. The quantity is distinct from a point-locus evaluation such as poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point, which evaluates a flux function at a specified position rather than integrating over a finite loop-bounded surface.

The defining surface is any oriented spanning surface with the same loop boundary and orientation; the absence of magnetic monopoles makes the linked flux independent of the particular spanning surface. This quantity is related to [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) as a loop-bounded flux linkage, and it must not be identified with [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which uses a different flux-surface geometry; a reconstructed counterpart, reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux of flux loop, shares the same magnetic quantity but represents a distinct value type when that distinction is made.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a positive net projection on the oriented surface element selected as positive for the flux loop.

examples.before:
Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is the toroidal conventional current density assigned to a closed magnetic-flux surface. It represents the total toroidal current-density component on that surface, expressed with the geometry weighting that provides the effective toroidal current source for the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux distribution.

The defining flux-surface average is

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}} = \frac{\left\langle j_\phi/R \right\rangle}{\left\langle 1/R \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{FSA}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density, $j_\phi$ is the local toroidal component of the conventional current-density vector projected on $\hat{\phi}$, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes an average over the closed magnetic-flux surface.

The scope is closed magnetic-flux surfaces in an axisymmetric equilibrium, and the aggregation is over the total conventional current carried by the plasma unless a population-specific qualifier is present. This quantity is not the unweighted flux-surface average of $j_\phi$, not a local current-density component at a point, and not a field-aligned or parallel current density.

It is the toroidal counterpart of the [parallel flux-surface-averaged current density] and a member of the [flux-surface-averaged current density] family. In equilibrium, this weighted toroidal average is the scalar source coupled to the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) in the Grad-Shafranov balance.

Sign convention: Positive when the conventional current-density vector has a positive projection on $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
